newsitem.title: CONGO: French soldier killed in Congo Brazzaville.
newsitem.headline: French soldier killed in Congo Brazzaville.

text.p: One French soldier has been killed and five wounded in the capital of Congo Brazzaville in a firefight with unruly Congolese soldiers during clashes fuelled by pre-election political and ethnic rivalry.

The French Defence Ministry in Paris said the soldier was shot dead on Saturday evening after a third day of bloodshed and confusion in the capital of the former French colony, across the Congo River from Laurent Kabila's Democratic Republic of Congo.
Earlier, a group of 44 U.S. citizens flew out of Brazzaville for Kinshasa, the capital of Kabila's Congo, with stories of bullets whistling near their plane.
"Shots were fired at the airplane and we saw red tracer bullets going past," Stan Hotelan, of the Christian Alliance Mission, told Reuters in Kinshasa across the Congo River.

A showdown pitting militiamen loyal to ex-president Denis Sassou Nguesso against soldiers loyal to President Pascal Lissouba and rival militia began on Thursday after Lissouba's government ordered a crackdown on private militias and unauthorised possession of weapons.
Soldiers surrounded the northern suburban home of Sassou Nguesso, a former Marxist military leader named president in 1979 but voted out of office in 1992 after the advent of democratic reform.
Sassou Nguesso has accused Lissouba, who won the 1992 presidential election, of fomenting violence to postpone a fresh election planned for July 27.
Government officials said troops had gone to his home to arrest members of his entourage on murder charges in connection with incidents in the north.

France said the soldier was shot dead when what it called "uncontrolled elements" of the Congolese army fired on them as they evacuated a group of foreign residents, including French nationals, who had been pinned down in a building by firing.
The ministry said the operation had approval from the Congolese authorities and that a senior officer in the Congolese army, who was with the French troops, was wounded.
Fighting between rival political and ethnic militias killed at least 2,000 people in the city in 1993.
Fighting in the north between supporters of Sassou Nguesso and former president and prime minister Jacques Joachim Yhombi Opango, Lissouba's campaign manager, has killed 16 people in under a month.

There was no reliable death toll for the Brazzaville clashes although police sources spoke of several dozen dead and many Lissouba, Sassou Nguesso and 1992 runner-up and Brazzaville mayor Bernard Kolelas are likely to be the front-runners among about a dozen hopefuls on July 27.
Lissouba's prime minister, Charles David Ganao, told state radio on Saturday night that the polls would go ahead as planned and called for a halt to fighting and looting in the city.
"Peace today is seriously disturbed. The Congolese have started killing each other again," he said.

He announced that Lissouba had accepted a mediation offer from Gabon's veteran president, Omar Bongo, and that a broad-based consultation between the government and the country's political class could begin as early as Sunday.
International telephone links were down. Telephone contacts remained possible through residents plugged into the mobile telephone network in Laurent Kabila's Congo to the south.
